extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Euclidean geometry (readers of Euclid's Elements, Books III–IV), geometry instructors and historians of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and commentary on Euclid's Book III–IV propositions about circles and circle constructions, including statements (e.g. angle in a semicircle), constructions (fitting/cutting segments, inscribing/circumscribing circles), and metamathematical guidance about cases and proof methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle in a semicircle is right (III.31)
rubrics_metrics.description: If ABC is a semicircle then the angle BAC (in a semicircle) is right.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs given via isosceles right-angled triangles and by noting that angles in the same segment are equal (III.21). Alternative proofs and historical variants are discussed; corollary about a triangle with one angle equal to the other two being right is noted (sometimes omitted in later texts). Commentary: Euclid's references to angles of segments greater/less than a semicircle are survivals of older controversies and not essential to elementary geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angles formed by a tangent and a chord equal angles in alternate segments (III.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a straight line EF touches circle ABCD at H and BD is a chord cutting the circle, then the angles which BD makes with the tangent EF are equal to the angles in the alternate segments of the circle (e.g., angle FBD equals angle in segment BAD).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof constructs diameter through point of contact and uses III.31 and III.22 (opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral equal to two right angles). The converse is also true: if a line through chord endpoint makes angles equal to the angles in alternate segments, it is a tangent. Historical notes: alternative direct proofs (Clavius) and indirect proofs (Camerer, Todhunter) are possible; special case where alternate segments are semicircles requires III.31.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct a circle segment on a given line admitting a given rectilineal angle (III.33)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given straight line AB and a rectilineal angle at C, construct on AB a segment of a circle whose inscribed angle equals the given angle (cases: angle at C acute, right, or obtuse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: at A construct angle equal to given angle, draw AE ⟂ AD, bisect AB at F, draw FG ⟂ AB, take G as center to draw circle through A and B (cases handled similarly for acute and obtuse; right angle case can be solved simply by bisecting AB and describing a semicircle). Notes: Simson observes first and third cases share same construction; Clavius's simpler bisecting method for right angle noted. Ensure AE and FG meet (existence of intersection must be justified).

rubrics_metrics.name: From a given circle cut off a segment admitting a given rectilineal angle (III.34)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given circle ABC and rectilineal angle at D, cut off from circle ABC a segment admitting an angle equal to the given rectilineal angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: draw tangent EF at B, on line FB construct angle FBC equal to given angle; by III.32 the angle in alternate segment BAC equals FBC, hence BAC equals given angle and segment BAC is cut off. Alternative method: double the angle at the centre (or draw a diameter when given angle is right).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersecting chords rectangle equality (III.35)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two straight lines AC and BD in a circle intersect at E, then the rectangle contained by AE and EC equals the rectangle contained by DE and EB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof treats case where chords pass through centre separately (trivial equality) and the general case by taking centre F, dropping perpendiculars FG, FN, using bisected segments and Euclid I.47 and I.5 to relate squares and rectangles. Simson's additional intermediate cases are noted; the proposition can be combined with the corollary of III.36 in one enunciation. Converse: if AO·OB = CO·OD then four points are concyclic (proved indirectly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of a point / secant–tangent theorem (III.36)
rubrics_metrics.description: If external point D has two lines to the circle — one cutting it (meeting at A and C) and one tangent at B — then the rectangle AD·DC equals the square on DB (tangent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof splits into case where secant passes through centre and where it does not, using centre F, perpendiculars, I.6 and I.47 to relate rectangles and squares. Historical remark: Greek geometers preferred separate proofs for limiting cases rather than deriving a limiting case from the general case; Euclid gives separate arguments accordingly. Also note methods to deduce BA·AE = CA·AF for two secants from same external point and treat tangent as limiting position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of constructions: justify intersections and meeting of lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever a construction assumes lines or circles meet (e.g., AE and FG will meet, or bisectors/ perpendiculars will meet), the proof must justify existence of those intersections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simson and Todhunter point out Euclid sometimes omits such justifications; remedies include case-by-case figures, contradiction via parallels (if perpendiculars don't meet they are parallel implying absurdities), or using axioms about angle sums being less than two right angles to force intersection. Don't tacitly assume intersections without proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle case distinctions explicitly (acute, right, obtuse)
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructions and proofs in circle geometry frequently split into cases depending on whether an angle is acute, right, or obtuse; these cases must be considered and shown to be covered by the construction or by separate constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simson notes acute and obtuse cases share the same construction; right-angle cases sometimes admit simpler constructions. Euclid sometimes omits separate case work; modern readers should either handle cases separately or show a single construction covers them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct vs indirect proof choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Euclid sometimes proves facts indirectly (reductio) where a direct argument is possible; either form is acceptable but they are stylistically different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Euclid uses indirect arguments to show a circle touches three lines in IV.4 but direct proofs exist (Simson). Note that indirect proofs often refer back to earlier propositions (e.g., III.16) while direct proofs may invoke the Porism to that proposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer limiting cases from general case without proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek geometers typically preferred giving separate proofs for limiting cases (e.g., tangent as limiting secant) rather than deducing them directly from the general case including them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: III.36 demonstrates this approach: Euclid gives a separate proof for the tangent (limiting) case instead of inferring it from the general secant case. When writing proofs, be explicit about limiting positions or provide a separate limiting-case argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use earlier propositions as dependencies (logical chaining)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs rely on previously established propositions (e.g., III.21 angles in same segment, III.22 opposite angles of cyclic quadrilateral, I.13, I.47 etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly cite the earlier results used (Euclid does so frequently). The commentary shows multiple cross-references: e.g., III.32 uses III.31 and III.22; parts of proofs appeal to I.4, I.5, I.6, I.47, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit a given straight line into a circle (IV.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: To fit into a given circle a straight line equal to a given straight line not greater than the diameter: if given length equals a chord along diameter it's immediate; otherwise construct appropriate circle with centre and radius equal to given length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are infinitely many solutions; extra constraints (parallel to given line, passing through a point) make the problem more difficult and require additional constructions (Pappus' methods, Apollonius' discussions). Commentary: choosing an extremity as fixed yields two solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe a circle in a triangle (IV.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bisect two angles of triangle ABC; their bisectors meet at D, drop perpendiculars DE, DF, DG to the sides; these distances are equal and a circle centered at D with that radius is inscribed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses congruent right triangles; Euclid uses indirect proof to show circle touches sides (contradiction if it cut them). Note: bisectors of all three angles concur at the incenter. Remarks: existence of intersections of bisectors is assumed; Simson inserts argument that bisectors must meet (otherwise they'd be parallel and give absurdities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumscribe a circle about a triangle (IV.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perpendicular bisectors of sides of triangle ABC meet at point F (inside, on, or outside triangle depending on triangle being acute/right/obtuse); F is circumcenter and circle of radius FA passes through vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: bisect AB and AC at D and E, draw DF, EF ⟂ AB, AC, prove AF = BF = CF. Cases treated: meeting within triangle (acute), on side (right), outside (obtuse). Simson's remark: Euclid sometimes omits justification that perpendicular bisectors meet—supply argument if required.
